extracted.intended_audience: prospective contributors, authors, playwrights, and literate readers of a periodical
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and selecting material for a moral, instructive periodical and for writing theatrical comedy that refines manners rather than merely shocking. Includes submission practices, editorial standards, and principles for satire and stage subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish contributors' papers entire and without alteration
rubrics_metrics.description: When a correspondent's paper deserves publication, it should be printed entire and without any alteration; the editor will publish it 'entire, and without any Alteration' and will add the author's name if they choose to subscribe it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor explains earlier practice of adapting contributions but now resolves to print such papers in their 'native Dress and Colours' because altering them would 'do them a manifest Hurt and Violence.' Promises to publish worthy submissions verbatim and to credit authors who sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invite a very broad range of contributors on set subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Give out subjects/themes of all kinds and invite persons of every station, temper, profession, sex, and disposition to contribute according to their talents and experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The call explicitly includes 'Scholars, Citizens, Courtiers, Gentlemen of the Town or Country, and all Beaux, Rakes, Smarts, Prudes, Coquets, Housewives,' etc., and asks contributors to apply their 'several and respective Talents or Genius's' to the subject, submitting 'by such a Time'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match subject to contributor's knowledge, experience and temperament
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributors should write on subjects that 'hit their Tempers, Humours, or Circumstances' or where their particular knowledge/experience makes them profitable to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor solicits pieces 'as the Subject given out hits their Tempers, Humours, or Circumstances, or may be made profitable to the Publick by their particular Knowledge or Experience', and asks for timely submissions (example: 'MONEY' within ten days).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not promote false or base methods in practical advice (e.g., trade)
rubrics_metrics.description: When offering instructional material (such as trade advice), avoid putting base or improper methods in a good light; do not gloss over vice as industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and cautions: 'Let not Noise be called Industry, nor Impudence Courage. Let not good Fortune be imposed on the World for good Management... Niggardliness is not good Husbandry, nor Generosity Profusion.' Editors should be 'very circumspect' in such provinces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire must not be mere humiliation or ill-natured shock
rubrics_metrics.description: Hooting, making a young person blush, or speaking shocking things for their own sake is not wit but ill nature and 'a Sterility of Brain'; repeated insolence is 'a Confirmation of very extraordinary Dulness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correspondents are urged to refrain from 'hooting a young Fellow out of Countenance' and from concluding buffoonry with 'what makes you blush?' The paper recommends against raillery aimed only to disoblige, and urges correction of habitual insolence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ridicule should target vice/criminality, not mere seriousness or unfashionableness
rubrics_metrics.description: Good ridicule is leveled at what is immoral or criminal rather than simply at seriousness, unfashionableness, or harmless oddity; 'I have endeavoured to make nothing Ridiculous that is not in some measure Criminal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editor contrasts earlier practice of ridiculing what is merely 'Unfashionable' with his rule to set up 'the Immoral Man as the Object of Derision.' The object is moral reform, not mere mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never choose an improper subject for ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject is improper for ridicule if it 'is apt to stir up Horrour and Commiseration rather than Laughter'; such topics (e.g., violations that provoke pity) should be avoided in comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit rule: 'a Subject is improper for Ridicule, if it is apt to stir up Horrour and Commiseration rather than Laughter.' The essay cites Terence as avoiding subjects like violations of the marriage-bed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy and the stage should promote virtue and refine manners
rubrics_metrics.description: The English stage ought to be regulated so that plays contribute to morality and the 'Reformation of the Age'; stage entertainments should leave audiences 'wiser and better' and not exclude virtuous persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that if English theatre resembled Greek/Roman regulation, it would recommend religion and government and make vice appear unamiable; suggests inspections and limitations to restrain licentiousness and make theatre serviceable to public virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake being merry for being lewd; avoid low-genius lewdness
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers of low genius often confuse merriment with lewdness; true comedy distinguishes between harmless mirth and indecency and must avoid lewd content that corrupts audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning that degenerate comedies 'know no difference between being Merry and being Lewd' and that indecent entertainments exclude many from the benefit of theatre, especially parents fearful for their children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scholarly trappings (e.g., Latin) honestly; don't rely on affectation to claim authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Employing learned devices (such as Latin mottos) may create an impression of scholarship, but editors/authors should not misuse such trappings to falsely signal superior learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote: the editor keeps a Latin sentence in his front and observed readers infer 'What a prodigious Scholar is this Man!'—a caution that such devices can mislead and should be used with care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content should provide real value—instruction or agreeable entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers should only take in the paper if, after perusal, they find themselves 'Two-pence the wiser, or the better Man for it'—each paper ought to give its price's worth in instruction or mirth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial standard expressed as advice to readers and writers: a paper must deliver a 'Two-pennyworth of Mirth or Instruction' to justify its cost and existence; this also justifies continuing publication despite increased price.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use irrelevant credentials or sensational provenance to impress
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of distant travel, strange accidents, or irrelevant family history are often used to create awe and improperly persuade the credulous; such signs do not constitute genuine authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of quack bills boasting of cures 'lately come from his Travels' or a surgeon who 'lost an Eye in the Emperor's Service' used to convince patients—advice to be skeptical of superficial proofs and to avoid such devices as writers.
